red.focus: Explain why Marbury v. Madison defines judicial authority.
red.summary: A court may recognize a right without having power to give the requested remedy. Learn how the 1803 Marbury decision connected judicial review with a written constitution.
checklist: I can identify what Marbury requested
I can distinguish right, remedy, and jurisdiction
I can explain the meaning of judicial review

sections.title: The undelivered commission
sections.body_md: William Marbury received a federal appointment near the end of President John Adams's administration, but his commission was not delivered before Thomas Jefferson took office. Marbury asked the Supreme Court to order Secretary of State James Madison to deliver it. His request presented a dispute about more than an official document. The Court also had to determine whether it possessed the lawful power to issue that particular order in the original proceeding.
sections.audio_script: William Marbury received a federal appointment near the end of President John Adams's administration, but his commission was not delivered before Thomas Jefferson took office. Marbury asked the Supreme Court to order Secretary of State James Madison to deliver it. His request presented a dispute about more than an official document. The Court also had to determine whether it possessed the lawful power to issue that particular order in the original proceeding.

sections.title: A right is not every remedy
sections.body_md: Chief Justice Marshall concluded that Marbury had a legal entitlement and that remedies could exist for its violation. The opinion nevertheless held that the Court could not grant the requested mandamus in its original jurisdiction. The Court treated the pertinent expansion of original jurisdiction under the Judiciary Act as inconsistent with Article III. These separate steps matter: possessing a right does not make every forum competent to enforce it in every form.

sections.title: The Constitution controls in a conflict
sections.body_md: Marbury became a foundational American articulation of judicial review: a court applying a written constitution treats it as superior to inconsistent ordinary legislation. It does not authorize judges everywhere to replace laws with personal opinions. The argument concerns legal hierarchy and the judiciary's responsibility in a concrete case. The student's task is to identify the actual legal sources, the jurisdictional question, and the narrow reason the Court could not issue the order Marbury sought.

yellow.focus: Analyze the precise reasoning and contested steps in Marbury.
yellow.summary: The opinion asks whether Marbury held a right, whether the law supplied a remedy, and whether the Court had jurisdiction. Examine why constitutional supremacy became central to the third answer.
checklist: I can reconstruct the opinion's three-question structure
I can state the Article III conflict
I can recognize contested interpretations of section 13

sections.title: Three questions, not one slogan
sections.body_md: Marshall examined whether the appointment was complete, whether violating the entitlement could have a remedy, and whether mandamus from the Supreme Court was legally available. The first two inquiries favored Marbury in the opinion, but the final jurisdictional question defeated his request. A legal analysis that jumps from the existence of a wrong directly to a desired judicial remedy ignores the independent problem of institutional competence.
sections.audio_script: Marshall examined whether the appointment was complete, whether violating the entitlement could have a remedy, and whether mandamus from the Supreme Court was legally available. The first two inquiries favored Marbury in the opinion, but the final jurisdictional question defeated his request. A legal analysis that jumps from the existence of a wrong directly to a desired judicial remedy ignores the independent problem of institutional competence.

sections.title: Reading the Judiciary Act
sections.body_md: The Court interpreted section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 as conferring original mandamus power beyond what Article III permitted. Because the Constitution controlled, the inconsistent statutory grant could not authorize the writ. Scholars debate whether that interpretation of the statute was compelled, making close reading essential. The student's answer should distinguish the Court's authoritative holding from historical and interpretive criticisms of its path to that result.

sections.title: The scope is not universal
sections.body_md: The U.S. system's model of constitutional review is influential but not the only model. Some countries use specialized constitutional courts or legislative responses, and constitutional hierarchy can operate differently. A lawyer must identify the judicial institution, binding sources, and available remedy in the relevant legal order. Marbury teaches an enduring question—who may declare the controlling legal norm—but its jurisdictional holding cannot simply be copied into every other constitution.

orange.focus: Compare American constitutional review with Miller in Britain.
orange.summary: Judicial enforcement of institutional boundaries does not require identical constitutions. Compare Marbury with the British Supreme Court's 2017 ruling about parliamentary authorization for European Union withdrawal.
checklist: I can state the legal issue in the first Miller decision
I can distinguish parliamentary sovereignty from American constitutional supremacy
I can identify the role of institutional restraint

sections.title: The executive could not decide alone
sections.body_md: In R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union (2017), the British Supreme Court considered whether ministers could initiate Article 50 withdrawal using prerogative power without parliamentary authorization. European Union rights had domestic legal effect through Parliament's legislation. The majority held that ministers could not use prerogative powers to change domestic law in that way without Parliament. The case did not decide whether leaving the Union was good policy; it decided who had legal authority.
sections.audio_script: In R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union (2017), the British Supreme Court considered whether ministers could initiate Article 50 withdrawal using prerogative power without parliamentary authorization. European Union rights had domestic legal effect through Parliament's legislation. The majority held that ministers could not use prerogative powers to change domestic law in that way without Parliament. The case did not decide whether leaving the Union was good policy; it decided who had legal authority.

sections.title: Same question, different architecture
sections.body_md: Marbury concerned a written federal constitution restricting a court's original jurisdiction and articulated constitutional supremacy. Miller concerned limits on executive prerogative and Parliament's authority over domestic legal change. Their doctrinal mechanisms differ, but both demand that public actors remain within the powers law grants them. It would be a mistake to say that Miller simply imported the American doctrine or that Marbury established British parliamentary sovereignty. Comparison must preserve the actual source of authority in each system.

sections.title: Judges may restrain without governing
sections.body_md: The British court required a legal authorization process but did not order Parliament to adopt any particular Brexit policy. The distinction illustrates how judicial intervention can protect the legislature's role rather than replace it. A mature analysis asks whether the court's reasoning identifies a legal boundary and whether its remedy stays within that boundary. Political consequences alone do not make a judgment unlawful; neither do political stakes expand a court's power.

black.focus: Justify judicial review in a democratic legal order.
black.summary: A court can defend constitutional boundaries while still raising questions about democratic legitimacy. Compare interpretive authority, institutional accountability, and the limits of judicial intervention.
checklist: I can evaluate democratic objections to judicial review
I can defend legally bounded institutional intervention
I can propose criteria for legitimate constitutional adjudication

sections.title: Who may settle a constitutional conflict?
sections.body_md: Marbury presents judicial review as part of deciding a case under superior constitutional law. Critics question whether unelected judges should control contested public policy; defenders argue that constitutional commitments protect people against ordinary political overreach. A doctoral account should distinguish interpretation of legal boundaries from selection of preferred policy. It must also consider how other institutions and the public can challenge serious judicial mistakes without making foundational limits meaningless.

It must also consider how other institutions and the public can challenge serious judicial mistakes without making foundational limits meaningless.

sections.title: Politics cannot be the entire test
sections.body_md: Miller had major political consequences but concerned a legal constraint on ministerial authority. Courts sometimes cannot avoid politically charged disputes without abandoning their assigned constitutional function. Yet a court's public importance does not justify extending its power beyond lawful questions. The relevant distinctions concern authoritative sources, scope of review, reasons given, and remedies. Institutional restraint means exercising required legal judgment without claiming unlimited authority over collective political choices.

sections.title: Judicial legitimacy requires reasons
sections.body_md: Design a framework demanding an identifiable legal controversy, careful examination of binding sources, candid treatment of disagreement, and remedies within judicial competence. Include practical access for people whose rights are affected and appropriate mechanisms for correcting mistakes. A system that automatically trusts every minister risks arbitrary executive action; a system that trusts every judge risks another concentration of power. Legitimate review demands public reasons answerable to law and to the people living under it.
